title: Is It Worth Your Budget? Formative Assessment Tools
author: Ashlee
summary: RatedEd reviews the paid tiers of six classroom formative assessment platforms, Quizizz, Pear Deck, Nearpod, Blooket, Gimkit and Kahoot, starting from the observation that each is free until a teacher needs it to do something. The business model, the review argues, depends on September adoption and November paywalls, by which point switching costs exceed upgrade costs. Before any ratings it raises the export question, whether teachers can take their question banks with them if they stop paying or the district switches, and calls it a whether-to-start question rather than a paid-tier one. Quizizz earns top marks for its free tier, Pear Deck for a paid tier that changes what the tool does, and Nearpod for teacher-paced lessons when a building pays. Blooket and Gimkit are praised for engagement but criticized for rewarding the game over the content, and Kahoot's shrinking free tier draws the weakest verdict. It closes with three questions for building leaders on renewal pricing, unused licenses and content ownership.
points: The review argues vendors win by locking in thirty class rosters before teachers hit paywalls later in the fall.
Whether teachers can export their question banks is framed as the first thing to check, before investing any time.
Only two of six upgrades are judged worth paying for: Pear Deck, and Nearpod when the building buys it.
Game-based tools like Blooket and Gimkit are recommended for review before an assessment, not as sources of instructional data.
Leaders are told to ask vendors for year-two renewal pricing and the share of purchased licenses that go unused.
quotes: Every one of these tools is free until the moment you need it to do something.
By then you have thirty class rosters in the platform and switching costs more than upgrading.
You will spend hours building question banks. Ask, before you invest that time: if I stop paying, or if my district switches platforms, can I take my questions with me in a usable format?
This is the one where paying changes the product rather than lifting a limit.

The game mechanics are the point and the assessment is the vehicle. Students often optimize for the game rather than the content, which is fine for review and poor for anything you plan to act on instructionally.
Raising a cap is not a feature. If you are hitting a cap, the first question is whether you are using the tool too much rather than whether you should pay more.
Your teachers are about to spend hundreds of collective hours building question banks. Find out who owns that work before they build it.
